unit.title: Cut, fit and install trunking system

summary: This unit teaches you to install trunking: the closed channels with removable lids that carry cables along walls, around offices and classrooms and through workshops. You will learn the types of PVC and steel trunking and their fittings, and how to plan, measure, mark out, cut, mitre, join and fix a run so that it is straight, level and secure. You will also learn to keep the earth path continuous on steel trunking, lay cables in safely, fit lids and fire barriers, and inspect and hand over the finished work.

blocks.p: **Trunking** is a closed channel, usually square or rectangular, with a lid that clips or screws on. Cables are laid into it rather than pulled through it, and more can be added later by taking off the lid. You will see it around office walls carrying power and data outlets, along classroom and laboratory walls, in workshops and plant rooms, and as risers in hotels and apartment blocks. This unit is for Level 2 trainees who cut, fit and install trunking under supervision.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it looks like on the job
rows: Work safely
Control sharp edges, dust, drilling into hidden services, work at height and existing live circuits; wear the right PPE.
Plan the run
Read the drawing for the route, size, height, outlets and fittings; measure the walls; note obstacles; list lengths and fittings.
Choose trunking and fittings
Pick the right type, material, size and fittings for the job and the place.
Measure, mark and cut
Mark a level line, mark cuts square, allow for fittings, cut square and mitred joints, and remove every burr.
Join and bend
Make neat mitres and joints, use factory fittings, and on steel trunking fit couplers and earth links.
Fix the trunking
Fix straight, level and plumb with the right screws, plugs and washers at the maker's spacing.
Lay cables and fit lids
Lay cables in neatly, keep power and data apart, do not overfill, support vertical runs, then fit lids and fire barriers.
Check earth continuity
Test a steel run end to end with a low-resistance ohmmeter and record the result.
Inspect, clean up and hand over
Check the work against the drawing, put faults right, clear and sort waste, and report.

ul: Many Jamaican offices, schools and shops are built of concrete block with concrete ceilings. Chasing cables into those walls is noisy, dusty and slow, so surface trunking is a common, tidy way to add or change circuits, especially in buildings that stay in use.

Under the US-based code used in Jamaica, metal trunking is called a **wireway** and small surface trunking a **surface raceway**. British drawings and suppliers say 'trunking'. They mean the same kind of product.
Heat and salt air matter. PVC trunking grows in the sun and softens if it gets too hot; steel trunking rusts near the sea unless it is galvanised or well painted.

blocks.note: Trunking is only as good as its workmanship: open mitres, sharp edges, lids that spring off and sagging runs are the first things an inspector or a customer notices. Work slowly enough to get each cut right.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Type
What it is like
Where it is used
rows: PVC mini-trunking
Small (for example 16 × 16 mm or 25 × 16 mm), often with a self-adhesive back as well as screw holes
A few cables run on the surface of a finished room: an extra outlet or light in a home, office or guest house
PVC trunking (standard)
From about 50 × 50 mm upwards, single or with a divider for two or more compartments
Classrooms, labs, offices, shops and light workshops
Dado and skirting trunking
Shaped PVC or aluminium trunking with two or three compartments; outlet boxes clip onto it
Around office walls at desk height (dado) or along the floor (skirting), carrying power and data to work stations
Steel trunking
Galvanised or painted sheet steel, single or multi-compartment, with couplers and screwed or clipped lids
Factories, workshops, plant rooms, risers and anywhere it may be knocked
Lighting trunking
Steel trunking that carries cables and also supports the light fittings hung from it
Warehouses, workshops and supermarkets
Underfloor trunking
Flat steel or PVC ducts laid in the floor screed, with outlet boxes at the surface
Open-plan offices where desks are away from walls

head: Point
PVC trunking
Steel trunking
rows: Strength
Fine where it will not be knocked; can crack or dent
Strong; protects cables against knocks and heavy loads
Weight and working
Light; easy to cut with a fine-tooth saw; cut edges are not sharp
Heavier; harder to cut; **cut edges are sharp** and must be filed
Corrosion
Does not rust: good in damp places and near the sea
Must be galvanised or painted, or it rusts, especially near the sea
Earthing
Does not conduct, so it needs no earthing; a separate earth conductor is run for the circuits
Conducts, so it **must be earthed**, with the earth path kept continuous at every joint
Heat and fire
Softens in heat; burning PVC gives off toxic, corrosive smoke
Does not soften; stands up better in a fire
Typical places
Homes, offices, classrooms, shops
Factories, workshops, plant rooms, risers

ul: The **base** (also called the body or back) is the part fixed to the wall. The **lid** (cover) clips or screws onto it.
Sizes are given in **millimetres**, width × depth, for example 50 × 50 or 100 × 50. Lengths are usually 2 m or 3 m.
A **divider** (segregation barrier) splits the inside into compartments, so power and data cables can share one run while kept apart.

blocks.p: Factory fittings make a run neat, strong and quick to install, and they keep the cables away from sharp edges. Site-made joints, such as mitres, are used where a fitting is not available or will not fit, and must be just as neat.

head: Fitting
What it does
rows: Internal angle
Turns the run around the **inside** of a corner, where two walls meet, or where a wall meets the ceiling
External angle
Turns the run around the **outside** of a corner, such as around a column or a box-out
Flat angle (flat bend)
Turns the run through 90° on the same flat surface, for example from along a wall to up the same wall
Flat tee
Lets a branch leave the main run at a right angle
Cross (four-way)
Joins four runs where they meet
Coupler (joint cover)
Joins two straight lengths end to end
Reducer
Joins trunking of two different sizes
End cap
Closes the open end of a run so cables are covered and dust, insects and fingers are kept out
Conduit adaptor (spout or flanged coupling)
Lets a conduit enter the side or end of the trunking
Box adaptor or outlet box
Lets a socket outlet, switch or data outlet be mounted on the trunking
Cable retainer (pin rack or strap)
Holds cables in place on vertical runs so their weight does not rest on the lid
Fire barrier (fire stop)
Seals the inside of the trunking where it passes through a fire-rated wall or floor
Copper earth link (bonding link)
Carries the earth path across each joint in steel trunking
Grommet or bush
Protects cables where they leave the trunking through a hole

blocks.note: Fittings from one maker's system rarely fit another maker's trunking properly. Use one system for the whole run, and check the fittings when they are delivered.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Sharp cut edges and burrs on steel trunking
Cut-resistant gloves when handling cut steel; file every edge smooth
Dust and chips from sawing, filing and drilling
Safety glasses for cutting and drilling; a dust mask and ear protection for drilling block and concrete
Drilling into hidden cables or pipes
Check the drawings; scan with a cable detector before drilling; drill only where marked
Falls when working high on a wall
A sound stepladder or platform on firm, level ground; never stand on the top step
Carrying 2 m and 3 m lengths
Carry long lengths with a partner; watch for people, light fittings and doorways
Existing circuits in a trunking you are working on
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead those circuits before you open the lid or add cables
Trips over off-cuts, tools and leads
Keep the floor clear; sweep up often
Saw slipping in a mitre box
Hold the work firmly; keep fingers clear of the blade; use steady strokes

blocks.note: When new cables go into trunking that already carries working circuits, the lid is not simply taken off while those circuits are live. Damaged insulation, loose joints or a bare conductor may be inside. Isolate, lock off, tag and prove dead the circuits in that trunking first, using a tester proved before and after.
blocks.label: Safety

flow: Read the drawing: route, trunking size and type, height, outlets, fittings
Walk and measure the route: walls, corners, columns, doors, windows
Note obstacles: pipes, air-conditioning units, beams, window sills
Decide where each fitting, joint and outlet goes
Plan joints so they do not fall at outlet boxes or right at corners
List the lengths and fittings, with a little spare
Report anything that does not match the drawing

blocks.p: If the route on the drawing is now blocked, for example by a new air-conditioning unit or a cupboard, do not just go behind or through it. Report it, and agree a new route with your supervisor, then mark the change on the drawing.

blocks.h: Worked example: listing lengths and fittings

blocks.p: A classroom run goes along two walls that meet at an internal corner. Wall A is 5.6 m from the door frame to the corner, and wall B is 4.1 m from the corner to a window. Each end of the run has an end cap. Trunking comes in 3 m lengths, and the drawing shows four outlet boxes on the run.

head: Item
Working
Quantity
rows: Trunking for wall A
5.6 ÷ 3 = 1.87, rounded up
2 lengths (0.4 m off-cut)
Trunking for wall B
4.1 ÷ 3 = 1.37, rounded up; the 0.4 m off-cut is too short to make up the 1.1 m needed after one full length
2 lengths
Internal angle
One corner
Couplers
One joint on each wall
End caps
One at each end of the run
Outlet boxes
From the drawing
Screws, washers and plugs
Counted from the maker's spacing, plus a few spares
As counted

blocks.p: Remember to take off the allowance the corner fitting needs when you cut, and plan where each joint falls so that it is not at an outlet box. Lids usually come with the lengths; check before ordering.

head: Job
Tools
rows: Measuring and marking
Tape measure, try square, combination or mitre square, protractor or sliding bevel for odd angles, spirit level, chalk line, pencil or fine marker
Cutting
Fine-tooth hacksaw or junior hacksaw, mitre box, file, deburring tool or knife; for steel, a nibbler for cut-outs
Holes
Hammer drill and masonry bits; drill and HSS bits for steel; knockout punch or hole saw for round entries
Joining and fixing
Screwdrivers, spanners, rivet gun and pop rivets (some steel systems), wall plugs, round-head screws and washers
Checking
Cable detector; low-resistance ohmmeter for steel runs

ul: Take the height from the drawing, measured from the **finished floor level**, at each end of each wall.

Join the marks with a level line, using a spirit level or laser, and snap a chalk line along it. Mark the top or the bottom edge of the trunking, and say which on your notes, so everyone works to the same edge.
Mark where each joint, fitting, outlet and fixing will go, and scan each fixing point with a detector.

blocks.p: Fittings take up part of the run. Some fit over the ends of the trunking, some fit inside them, and the maker's instructions say how far short of a corner or tee to stop the trunking. Measure to that point, not to the corner itself.

blocks.note: Example: the maker's internal angle covers the trunking ends, and the trunking must stop 25 mm short of the corner on each wall. The run from the door frame to the corner is 2,750 mm. Cut the length to 2,750 − 25 = **2,725 mm**.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Measure twice, cut once. Mark the cut on the base with a **try square**, carry the line round both sides, so the cut is square (at 90°) all round.

Count the lengths needed for each wall: divide the wall length by the length of one piece and round up. A 6.4 m wall with 3 m lengths needs 6.4 ÷ 3 = 2.13, so 3 lengths, with an off-cut to use elsewhere.
Cut lids the same way, but plan their joints separately (see joints).
Use a **fine-tooth hacksaw** or junior hacksaw. Coarse teeth chip and crack thin PVC.
Hold the trunking firmly in a **mitre box**, which guides the saw for true 90° and 45° cuts. Keep the base flat in the box.
Use steady strokes with light pressure, keeping the saw upright.
Remove the whiskers of plastic and rough edges with a file, deburring tool or knife.
Wear **cut-resistant gloves and safety glasses**.

Use a hacksaw with a fine blade. **The thinner the metal, the finer the blade**, so that more than one tooth is always on the metal (on thicker work, aim for at least three). For thin sheet such as trunking, use the finest common blade, about **32 teeth per 25 mm (32 TPI)**; coarser blades straddle the sheet, snag and break their teeth.
Clamp or hold the trunking so it cannot move. Support the off-cut so it does not tear the last of the cut.
**File off every burr and sharp edge**, inside and out. Burrs cut cable insulation and hands.

Use a nibbler for rectangular cut-outs and a knockout punch or hole saw for round holes. An angle grinder makes sparks and burns off the zinc coating: use it only if your supervisor allows, with a permit where needed.

blocks.p: A mitre is a joint where two pieces are cut at matching angles, so they meet in a neat corner. Each piece is cut at **half of the change in direction**.

head: The run turns through
Cut each piece at
Example
rows: A flat bend around a corner on the same wall
Following a wall that changes direction by 45°
A small change in direction

flow: Measure each piece to the corner, inside or outside edge as the drawing needs
Mark the angle across the base, using a mitre square, protractor or sliding bevel
Cut the first piece in the mitre box with steady, upright strokes
Cut the second piece at the opposite angle
Deburr both cuts
Dry-fit on the wall and check for gaps
Trim or re-cut until the joint is tight
Fix both pieces close to the joint, then cut the lid to match

blocks.note: A gap at a mitre comes from a cut that is not at the true angle, or not square across the base. Do not fill it with sealant or tape: re-cut the piece. A tight mitre is a sign of good work.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: Butt straight lengths together on the wall, in line and level, and cover the joint with a coupler (joint cover) where the system has one.
Fix each length close to the joint so the ends cannot lift or move apart.
Place the **lid joints away from the base joints** (staggered). The lid then bridges each base joint, which makes the run stronger and neater and stops a weak point where everything breaks at once.
Long PVC runs in hot places grow and shrink. Follow the maker's advice on leaving a small gap at couplers or fitting expansion couplers.
Cut lengths square, file the ends and butt them together in line.
Fit the coupler inside or over the joint and fix it with the screws, nuts and bolts or pop rivets the maker supplies, so that the joint is tight and cannot move.
For a tee, fit the factory tee into the run with its couplers, or cut the side of the main run for the branch exactly as the maker's instructions say.

blocks.h: The earth path in steel trunking

blocks.p: Steel trunking that carries cables must be **earthed**. If a cable's insulation is damaged and its line conductor touches the trunking, the fault current must flow back along an unbroken earth path so the breaker or fuse trips at once. If the path is broken at a joint, everything beyond it could stay live, and anyone touching it could get a shock.

ul: A coupler alone is not a reliable earth path: paint, zinc oxide and loose screws can break it.
Fit a **copper earth link** across **every** joint, including each joint of a tee or cross, bolted to the trunking on both sides.
Make clean **metal-to-metal contact**: scrape off paint or dirt under the link, and use the serrated (shakeproof) washers supplied.

Connect the run to the main earth as the drawing shows. Whether the trunking itself may serve as the circuits' protective conductor depends on the code and the drawing; many designers run a separate earth conductor as well.

flow: Make sure the run is dead and no circuits are connected to it
Zero (null) the leads of the low-resistance ohmmeter
Measure from one end of the run to the other, and to each branch
Check that the reading is low, as the test sheet requires
If it is high, test joint by joint to find the bad link
Put it right, retest and record the result

blocks.p: A good run reads a small fraction of an ohm. A reading that jumps across one joint points to a missing, loose or painted-over earth link there. Looking at a run or knocking on it tells you nothing: only the meter proves continuity.

flow: Hold the base on the level line and mark the holes through it
Take it down; scan each hole position with a detector
Drill with a masonry bit of the size the plug needs, wearing glasses, mask and ear protection
Clean the dust out and push in wall plugs that suit the screws
Fix with round-head or pan-head screws and washers
Check level along the length and that joints are tight and in line

ul: Fix at the **maker's spacing**, with a fixing **close to each end** of every length so the ends cannot lift and the joints cannot open.
Example: a 3 m length with fixings every 600 mm and one at each end has 3,000 ÷ 600 = 5 spaces, so 6 fixings.
Use **round-head or pan-head screws with washers** on PVC. The flat underside spreads the load. A countersunk screw acts like a wedge and splits or cracks the PVC base.
Steel trunking may need holes drilled or punched in the base if it has none. Deburr them.
Do not over-tighten screws in PVC: it distorts the base and the lid will not clip on.

head: Surface
Fixing
rows: Timber
Wood screws with washers into solid timber
Drywall or ceiling board
Hollow-wall anchors for light runs; heavy runs fixed through to studs or the structure
Steel frames or purlins
Self-drilling screws, or bolts through drilled holes
Mini-trunking
Its self-adhesive strip helps to hold it while you fix it, but add screws: adhesive alone lets go on dusty, damp or painted walls, especially in heat

ul: Make round holes for box entries with a **knockout punch or hole saw**, never by hammering a chisel through. Deburr the hole.
Fit a **grommet or bush** in any hole where cables leave the trunking.
Use a **conduit adaptor** where conduit joins the trunking.
Fit outlet boxes and box adaptors at the heights and positions on the drawing, with the trunking joints planned to fall away from them.

sections.title: Laying cables, fitting lids and fire safety

ul: Joints tight, edges filed, grommets fitted, earth links in place on steel runs.
Any circuits already in the trunking isolated, locked off and proved dead.
The cable schedule or drawing to hand, so each cable goes to the right place.
Lay cables in side by side, neatly, without twisting them or crossing them more than you must.
Do not drag cables over sharp edges or pull them tight round fittings.
Keep to each cable's minimum bending radius at angles and tees. Data cables are easily damaged by tight bends: large-radius corner fittings are often specified for the data compartment.
Label circuits where they enter and leave the trunking.

blocks.p: Power cables and data, telephone, alarm or other low-voltage cables must be **segregated**: kept in separate compartments, separated by the divider, or in separate trunking. This protects the low-voltage system from mains voltage if insulation fails, and reduces interference on data signals. Both the US-based code used in Jamaica and British rules require it. A missing divider is fitted before any cables go in.

Cables bunched in trunking cannot lose their heat as easily as cables on their own, so they run hotter. Overfilled trunking also makes the lid press on the cables, and leaves no room to add more later. The **space factor** is the share of the trunking's inside cross-section taken up by the cables.

head: Rule
Limit
rows: British practice for trunking
Cables fill no more than **45%** of the inside area
NEC rule for wireways (metal or non-metal trunking)
Conductors fill no more than **20%** of the inside area

blocks.p: Follow the rule the drawing and your supervisor give. Worked example at 45%: a compartment 50 × 50 mm has an inside area of only about 2,200 mm², because the walls and lid take some space. 45% of that is about 990 mm². If each cable takes up 30 mm² (from the maker's table of overall areas), up to 990 ÷ 30 = 33 cables fit. Where many circuits share a trunking, the designer may also choose larger cables, because grouped cables must carry less current each (they are **derated**).

On a vertical run the cables' weight pulls them down. Fit **cable retainers** (pin racks or straps) at the spacing the maker gives, so the weight rests on the retainers, not on the lid or the cables at the top bend.

ul: Fit lids **after** the cables are in and have been checked.
Fit lids all along the run and clip or screw them fully home, so cables are protected and fingers kept out.
Cut lids neatly to fit close to outlet boxes and fittings, with no gaps.
If a lid will not clip on, the cables are bulging: find out why. Never force a lid onto cables; it can crush them.

blocks.p: Where trunking passes through a **fire-rated** wall or floor, such as into a stairwell, a plant room or between apartments, fire and smoke could travel along it. Two things are needed:

ul: A **fire barrier** inside the trunking at the wall or floor, fitted as the maker says.
**Fire-stopping** around the outside of the trunking, sealing the gap between the trunking and the hole in the wall with an approved fire-stopping material.

blocks.note: Never leave a fire-rated wall or floor with an open hole around trunking, and never pack it with ordinary foam, paper or rags. A missing fire stop can let smoke fill a stairwell that people need to escape by.
blocks.label: Safety

head: Check
What good looks like
rows: Against the drawing
Route, size, height and outlet positions as drawn, or changes agreed and marked
Line
Straight, level and plumb; no sags or kinks
Fixings
Every length firm, a fixing near each end, spacing as the maker says
Joints and mitres
Tight, in line, no gaps; lid joints staggered from base joints
Edges
No burrs or sharp edges anywhere
Lids
Fitted all along, fully clipped or screwed, neat at fittings and outlets
Cables
Neat, not overfilled, power and data segregated, retainers on vertical runs, grommets where they leave
Steel runs
Earth link across every joint; continuity tested and recorded
Fire safety
Fire barriers and fire-stopping at fire-rated walls and floors
Labels and area
Circuits labelled; area clean; off-cuts cleared

head: Fault
Likely cause
Cure
rows: Gap at a mitre
Cut not at the true angle or not square
Re-cut the piece
Lid springs off
Base distorted by over-tight screws, or cables overfilling
Loosen and refix; re-lay cables or fit larger trunking
Ends lifting at joints
No fixing close to the end
Add fixings near each end
Run wavy or out of level
No chalk line, or fixed by eye
Refix to a level line
High continuity reading on steel
Missing, loose or painted-over earth link
Clean, refit and retest
Cracked PVC base at fixings
Countersunk screws or no washers
Replace the length; use round-head screws and washers

ul: Sweep up during the job and at the end. PVC off-cuts and screws cause trips; steel off-cuts and swarf cut hands and feet.
Store trunking **flat and supported, out of direct sun**: PVC sags and warps in heat, and long lengths standing up can fall on someone.
Sort waste: clean PVC and steel off-cuts for reuse or recycling where possible; the rest in the right bins. **Never leave off-cuts inside trunking.**
**Never burn PVC.** Burning PVC gives off hydrogen chloride and other toxic gases that harm the lungs and corrode metal.

blocks.p: Report to your supervisor that the run is complete and checked, with the continuity results for steel runs, any problems found, and any change to the route marked on the drawing for the as-built record.
Tick each statement only when you can do it without looking at the notes.

ul: I can say what trunking is and why it is used instead of conduit in some jobs.
I can describe mini, standard, dado, skirting, steel, lighting and underfloor trunking and where each is used.
I can compare PVC and steel trunking.
I can name the main fittings and say what each one does.
I can name the hazards of trunking work and the controls, including isolation of circuits already in a trunking.
I can plan a run from the drawing and list the lengths and fittings.
I can mark a level line, mark square cuts and allow for fittings when measuring.
I can choose a saw blade and cut PVC and steel trunking square, and remove all burrs.
I can work out a mitre angle and cut a tight mitre in a mitre box.
I can join steel trunking with couplers and fit an earth link across every joint.
I can test the earth continuity of a steel run and explain a high reading.
I can fix trunking level and secure with the right screws, washers and plugs at the maker's spacing.
I can lay cables in without overfilling, keep power and data apart, and support vertical runs.
I can fit lids correctly and explain fire barriers and fire-stopping.
I can inspect a finished run, put faults right, clear up waste safely and report.

head: Figure
What it is
rows: Half the change in direction
The angle to cut each piece of a mitre: 45° for a 90° turn
About 32 TPI
Hacksaw blade for thin sheet steel such as trunking
Thinner metal, finer blade
The rule for choosing a hacksaw blade
British space factor limit for trunking
NEC fill limit for wireways
Spaces + 1
Fixings on a length with one at each end
2 m or 3 m
Usual trunking lengths

terms: Base
The part of the trunking fixed to the wall, under the lid.
Conduit adaptor
A fitting that lets conduit enter the side or end of trunking.
Coupler
A fitting that joins two lengths of trunking end to end.
Derating
Reducing the current a cable may carry, for example because it is grouped with other cables.
Earth link
A copper strap fitted across a joint in steel trunking to keep the earth path continuous.
External angle
A fitting that turns a run around the outside of a corner.
Fire barrier
A seal fitted inside trunking where it passes through a fire-rated wall or floor.
Fire-stopping
Approved material that seals the gap around a service passing through a fire-rated wall or floor.
Internal angle
A fitting that turns a run around the inside of a corner.
Mitre
A joint where two pieces are cut at matching angles to meet in a corner.
Mitre box
A guide that holds the work and the saw for accurate 45° and 90° cuts.
Segregation
Keeping power cables apart from data and other low-voltage cables.
Space factor
The share of the inside cross-section of trunking that is filled by cables.
Wireway
The NEC name for metal or non-metal trunking with a removable cover.

c1.title: Dado trunking in a New Kingston office
c1.text: Trainee Jhanelle Watson and electrician Mr Robert Chin are installing three-compartment PVC dado trunking around the walls of an insurance office in New Kingston, Kingston. Each desk will have power outlets and data outlets mounted on the trunking. One compartment is for power, one for data and one for telephone and alarm cables. A data cabling contractor is working alongside them. The job specification sets a space factor of 45% for the trunking.

c2.title: A computer lab in Falmouth
c2.text: Trainee Odane Mitchell and electrician Mrs Yvonne Daley are fitting 50 × 50 mm PVC trunking around a computer lab at a high school in Falmouth, Trelawny. The run has an internal corner, a flat bend around a window that must be site-made as a mitre, and a section where one wall changes direction by 45°. The maker's internal angle covers the trunking ends, and the trunking must stop 25 mm short of the corner on each wall.

c3.title: Steel trunking in a Downtown Kingston print shop
c3.text: Trainee Tyrone Barnes and electrician Ms Claudette Hylton are installing 100 × 50 mm galvanised steel trunking along a wall above the machines in a printing works in Downtown Kingston. The run has four straight joints and a factory tee for a branch down to a paper guillotine. The steel is 1.2 mm thick. After fitting, they test the earth continuity from end to end.

c4.title: Mini-trunking in a Port Maria guest house
c4.text: Trainee Kemar Simpson and electrician Mr Owen Wint are adding outlets and a ceiling light in an old stone house that has been turned into a guest house in Port Maria, St Mary. The owner does not want any walls chased, so the new cables will run in PVC mini-trunking with a self-adhesive back. The run goes up a wall and onto the ceiling to the new light. Some of the walls are dusty and slightly damp.

c5.title: A riser in a Montego Bay hotel
c5.text: Trainee Nadine Robinson and electrician Mr Leroy Dixon are installing steel trunking that runs along a service corridor of a hotel in Montego Bay, St James, then through a fire-rated wall into a stairwell, and up the stairwell as a riser to the floors above. Twelve circuits will share the riser. The 3 m lengths are delivered to the ground floor.

questions.q: Where should Jhanelle plan the joints in the base of the dado trunking?
o: Exactly where each outlet box will go
Right at the corners of each wall
Away from the desk outlet boxes
Wherever the 3 m lengths happen to end
questions.why: A joint under an outlet box makes the box hard to fit and weakens the run where people push plugs in. Plan the lengths so joints fall between outlets, and away from the corner fittings.

questions.q: One length of trunking arrives without its divider, and the data cabler wants to lay his data cables in with the power cables there. What should Jhanelle say?
o: No; fit the divider first, as power and data must stay apart
Yes, as long as the data cables are a different colour
Yes, as long as the data cables are tied on top of the power
Yes, for one length only, since it is just a short section
questions.why: Power and data must be segregated along the whole run, not most of it. If mains insulation failed, the data cables and the equipment on them could become live, and the power cables also cause interference. The missing divider is fitted before any cables go in.

questions.q: The power compartment has an inside area of about 1,400 mm². Each power cable takes up 25 mm². At the 45% space factor, about how many cables may it hold?
questions.why: 45% of 1,400 mm² is 630 mm². 630 ÷ 25 = 25.2, so no more than 25 cables. Using the full 1,400 mm² (56 cables) would overfill it, so the cables would run hot and the lid would press on them.

questions.q: Why does the data contractor ask for the large-radius corner fittings in the data compartment instead of tight site-made mitres?
o: Large-radius fittings are the only ones that take a divider
Bends tighter than its minimum radius damage data cable
Site-made mitres are not allowed anywhere in PVC trunking
Tight corners make data cables carry mains interference
questions.why: Every cable has a minimum bending radius, and data cables are especially sensitive: bending them too tightly changes their construction and spoils their performance. Large-radius fittings keep the bend gentle.

questions.q: Where one wall changes direction by 45°, Odane will join two pieces with a mitre. At what angle should he cut each piece?
questions.why: Each piece of a mitre is cut at half the change in direction. A 90° turn needs two 45° cuts; a 45° turn needs two 22.5° cuts. Set the angle with a protractor or sliding bevel.

questions.q: The run from the door frame to the internal corner measures 2,750 mm. What length should Odane cut for this piece?
questions.why: The trunking must stop 25 mm short of the corner because the internal angle covers the ends. So 2,750 − 25 = 2,725 mm. Cutting to the full 2,750 mm would leave the fitting with nowhere to go.

questions.q: Odane's PVC cuts leave rough whiskers of plastic on the edges. What should he do before fitting the pieces?
o: Clean them off with a file or deburring tool
Leave them, because the lid will cover them over
Melt them smooth with a lighter or a heat gun
Wrap insulating tape around each of the cut ends
questions.why: Rough edges stop joints closing tightly, look poor and can nick cable insulation. A file, deburring tool or knife removes them cleanly. Heating PVC with a flame scorches it and gives off harmful fumes.

questions.q: When Odane dry-fits the mitred flat bend around the window, there is a 3 mm gap at the outer corner. What is the right fix?
o: Fill the gap with white sealant so it does not show
Push the two pieces hard together as he screws them
Re-cut the piece so the angle is true and square
Cover the gap with a short strip of insulating tape
questions.why: A gap shows that a cut was not at the true angle or not square across the base. Forcing it distorts the run; filler and tape are poor work and fail. Re-cut carefully in the mitre box until the joint is tight.

questions.q: Which hacksaw blade is best for cutting the 1.2 mm steel trunking?
o: A coarse blade of about 14 TPI
A wood saw with large teeth
A medium blade of about 18 TPI
A fine blade of about 32 TPI
questions.why: The thinner the metal, the finer the blade must be, so that more than one tooth is always on the metal. A coarse blade straddles thin sheet, snags and strips its teeth; the finest common blade, about 32 teeth per 25 mm, cuts it cleanly.

questions.q: Before bolting an earth link across a joint, Tyrone finds the coupler area is dusty and has a spot of paint. What should he do?
o: Bolt the link over the paint, since the bolts cut through it
Scrape it to clean, bare metal and use the serrated washers
Leave out the link, as the coupler already joins the metal
Wrap the joint in insulating tape to keep the dust off it
questions.why: An earth link needs clean metal-to-metal contact on both sides. Paint and dirt add resistance that can stop fault current tripping the protection. Serrated washers bite through any thin film and stop the bolts loosening.

questions.q: How many copper earth links does the factory tee need where it joins the run?
o: One across each of its three joints
One for the whole tee, on its branch
None, as the tee is a single pressing
Two, one on each side of the main run
questions.why: The earth path must be unbroken into every leg of the run. A tee is joined to the trunking at three places, so each joint gets its own link, bolted to clean metal on both sides.

questions.q: The end-to-end continuity reading is very high. Testing joint by joint, the reading jumps across the third joint. What is the most likely cause?
o: The trunking run is too long to give a low reading
The ohmmeter leads were not zeroed before the test began
That joint's earth link is missing, loose or on paint
The tee branch is draining current from the run
questions.why: A sudden rise across one joint points to a poor connection there: a missing link, a loose bolt or a link fitted over paint or dirt. Put it right, retest the whole run and record the reading.

questions.q: The mini-trunking has a self-adhesive back. How should Kemar fix it to the dusty, slightly damp walls?
o: Rely on the adhesive alone, as the owner wants no holes
Glue it with extra contact adhesive and no screws
Use the adhesive to position it, and screw it as well
Tape it to the wall until the adhesive has set firmly
questions.why: Self-adhesive backing alone often lets go on dusty, damp or painted walls, especially in the heat, and the run then sags or falls with the cables in it. Screws with plugs at the maker's spacing hold it permanently.

questions.q: Which fitting should Kemar use where the run goes from the wall onto the ceiling?
o: An internal angle
An external angle
A flat tee fitting
A flat angle bend
questions.why: Where the wall meets the ceiling, the trunking turns around the inside of the corner, so an internal angle is used. An external angle goes around the outside of a corner, such as a column.

questions.q: Near the end of the run, the mini-trunking lid will not clip on because the cables bulge out. What should Kemar do?
o: Press the lid on hard with a block of wood and a mallet
Re-lay the cables, or fit larger trunking if too full
Leave the lid off that part, since it is out of reach
Tape the lid down along the run where it will not clip
questions.why: A lid that will not close means the cables are badly laid or the trunking is overfilled. Forcing the lid can crush the cables. Lay them flat and neat; if they still do not fit, a larger size is needed.

questions.q: Nadine has fitted the fire barrier inside the trunking at the stairwell wall. What must also be done to the hole in the wall around it?
o: Fit an extra earth link on each side of the wall
Leave the gap open so the cables can lose heat
Pack the gap with ordinary foam from a can
Seal the gap around it with fire-stopping
questions.why: Fire and smoke can pass through the gap around the trunking as well as through the inside. Approved fire-stopping seals the hole so the wall keeps its fire rating, protecting the stairwell people use to escape.

questions.q: Twelve circuits share the riser. Why might the designer specify larger cables than for one circuit on its own?
o: Grouped cables run hotter, so each must be derated
Larger cables are easier to lay into steel trunking
Steel trunking cuts the voltage on each cable it holds
Larger cables need fewer earth links on the riser
questions.why: Cables bunched together cannot lose heat as easily as a single cable, so each one may carry less current. To carry the same load safely, the designer chooses a larger size.

questions.q: How should the 3 m lengths of steel trunking be moved up the stairwell?
o: One person, carrying each length upright up the stairs
One person, dragging each length up the stairs by one end
Thrown up to a helper on the landing above to save time
Two people, one at each end, watching the way ahead
questions.why: Long, heavy lengths are awkward on stairs and can hit people, walls and light fittings. Two people sharing the load, one at each end, can steer them safely. Dragging damages the trunking and the stairs.

questions.q: Why must PVC trunking off-cuts never be burnt on site?
o: Burnt PVC can no longer be sold for scrap
PVC burns too slowly to be worth the time
It gives off toxic, corrosive gases
Burnt PVC leaves ash that blocks the drains
questions.why: Burning PVC releases hydrogen chloride and other toxic gases that harm the lungs and eyes and corrode metal. Put off-cuts in the right bin for reuse, recycling or disposal.

questions.q: On drawings that follow the NEC, what is metal trunking with a removable cover called?
o: A busway
A wireway
A cable tray
A conduit body
questions.why: The NEC calls metal (and non-metal) trunking with a removable cover a wireway, and small surface trunking a surface raceway. A busway carries bare or insulated bars, a cable tray is open, and a conduit body is a fitting on a conduit run.
